title: DNS-Based Load Balancing
description: Learn how DNS-based load balancing works, its limitations, and how it fits into a larger multi-tier load balancing strategy.

data.text: DNS-based load balancing uses the Domain Name System to distribute traffic across multiple servers or regions. When a client resolves a domain name, the DNS resolver returns one of several IP addresses. The choice of IP can be based on geography, server health, or simple round-robin rotation.

A DNS load balancer maintains a list of IP addresses for a domain. Each time a resolver queries the domain, the load balancer selects an address using a configured policy. Because DNS is cached by resolvers and operating systems, the actual distribution of traffic depends on TTL values and client behavior.

data.title: Caching Impact
data.text: Low TTL values improve responsiveness to failures, but they increase DNS query volume. High TTL values reduce query volume but slow failover.

data.title: DNS load balancing policies
items: Round robin: return addresses in sequential order.
Weighted round robin: return addresses based on assigned weights.
Geo-based: return the closest regional address.
Latency-based: return the address with the lowest measured latency.

data.text: DNS load balancing does not provide true load awareness because resolvers cache responses. It also cannot react to server failures instantly. For these reasons, DNS is often combined with a local load balancer or CDN rather than used as the sole traffic distribution mechanism.

cards.title: DNS Load Balancing
cards.description: Routes traffic before TCP connection is established. Low overhead but cache-dependent.

cards.title: Local Load Balancing
cards.description: Routes each request or connection actively. Better health visibility but adds infrastructure complexity.

data.title: Takeaway
points: DNS load balancing distributes traffic at name resolution time.
Caching makes it efficient but less responsive to failures.
It works best as part of a multi-tier routing strategy.
data.takeaway: Use DNS load balancing for broad traffic distribution and combine it with active local load balancing for resilience.
